steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing a semantic association rule learning approach that combines time series data with knowledge graphs in a digital twin setting. Introduce association rule mining for IoT data, state our hypothesis, explain digital twins and knowledge graphs, and list our contributions and the evaluation use case.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Learning rules and patterns from data is one of the core sub-fields in data analysis and machine learning. Association Rule Mining (ARM) is a specific task in rule learning, and the goal is to learn association rules between variables that describe how two or more variables are associated with each other. In an industrial Internet of Things (IoT) setting, ARM methods are used to learn rules from time series sensor data.

Association rules have the form X\rightarrow Y, which means that if X holds, then Y also holds, and X and Y can be a single variable or multiple variables with a truth value. Many approaches have been proposed to apply ARM methods to numerical data, including discretization, optimization and statistical approaches, and they go under the name Numerical ARM or Quantitative ARM. For example, for time series data that IoT devices produce, a simple association rule based on a statistical approach can have the form \text{mean}(m_{t}^{X})\rightarrow\text{mean}(n_{t}^{Y}), which is interpreted as "in a time frame t, if mean measurement from sensor X is m, then the mean value of the measurements of sensor Y must be n". Discretization methods means discretizing the numerical data before an ARM algorithm is run. Optimization methods means evolutionary algorithms where rule quality criteria are usually used as fitness functions to learn rules in a desired format.

- Hypothesis; Digital Twins and Knowledge Graphs
  - hypothesis: semantics of system components helps rule learning on industrial IoT numerical data - unknown relations (more rules), generalizing rules of above form
  - tested in a Digital Twin (DT)
  - many DT definitions over past two decades
  - goal: precise representation ('twin') of physical system (Physical Twin, PT) in digital environment, bi-directional communication
  - semantic technologies (ontologies, Knowledge Graphs) recently used in DTs: system/data modeling, semantic interoperability, semantic relations, reasoning
- Gap and contributions
  - no approach for learning rules with semantic info + time series data in a DT
  - first semantic rule learning approach using KGs, based on FP-Growth
  - full pipeline: KG construction in DTs, semantic ARM from KG + time series, inference from learned rules (Section 2)
  - Naive SemRL: extends FP-Growth (Section 3)
  - semantic rule quality measure (Section 4)

  - ongoing research, open issues and research questions in Section 5

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Learning rules and patterns from data is one of the core sub-fields in data analysis and machine learning. Association Rule Mining (ARM) is a specific task in rule learning, and the goal is to learn association rules between variables that describe how two or more variables are associated with each other. In an industrial Internet of Things (IoT) setting, ARM methods are used to learn rules from time series sensor data.

Association rules have the form X\rightarrow Y, which means that if X holds, then Y also holds, and X and Y can be a single variable or multiple variables with a truth value. Many approaches have been proposed to apply ARM methods to numerical data, including discretization, optimization and statistical approaches, and they go under the name Numerical ARM or Quantitative ARM. For example, for time series data that IoT devices produce, a simple association rule based on a statistical approach can have the form \text{mean}(m_{t}^{X})\rightarrow\text{mean}(n_{t}^{Y}), which is interpreted as "in a time frame t, if mean measurement from sensor X is m, then the mean value of the measurements of sensor Y must be n". Discretization methods means discretizing the numerical data before an ARM algorithm is run. Optimization methods means evolutionary algorithms where rule quality criteria are usually used as fitness functions to learn rules in a desired format.

Our hypothesis is that for numerical data produced in industrial IoT networks, it can be beneficial to include the semantics of the system components in rule learning. This includes discovering relations that were not known before, e.g. a higher number of rules, and helping to generalize association rules of the form above. We test this hypothesis in a specific type of IoT scenario, which is a Digital Twin (DT). Many different definitions of DTs have been proposed over the past two decades. The main goal is to create a precise representation (a 'twin') of a physical system, which is often called the Physical Twin (PT), in a digital environment, and to keep a bi-directional communication between them. Recently semantic technologies like ontologies and Knowledge Graphs (KGs) have started to be used in DTs, for system/data modeling, for establishing semantic interoperability, for extracting semantic relations and/or for facilitating reasoning processes.

As far as we know, at the time of writing there is no approach that learns rules containing semantic information as well as time series data in a DT. This study tries to fill this gap. We propose a first semantic rule learning approach that uses KGs and is based on the well-known FP-Growth algorithm. The contributions of this paper are:

- A full pipeline of operations, which consists of: i) KG construction in DTs, ii) semantic association rule learning based on the KG and time series data, and iii) making inferences based on the learned rules (Section 2).

- A first approach (Naive SemRL) that extends the FP-Growth algorithm to learn rules that contain semantic information from KGs and time-series data (Section 3).

- A semantic rule quality measure to evaluate the rules that semantic rule learning algorithms generate (Section 4).

We evaluate the proposed approach in an industrial use case, water networks. Water networks are water distribution systems that bring water to consumers, i.e. apartments, industrial sites. This is ongoing research and there are many open issues and research questions, which we emphasize in Section 5.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Learning rules and patterns from data is one of the core sub-fields in data analysis and machine learning. Association Rule Mining (ARM) is one specific task in rule learning where the goal is to learn association rules between variables, which describe how two or more variables are associated with each other. In an industrial Internet of Things (IoT) setting, ARM methods are used to learn rules from time series sensor data [1,2].

Association rules are in the form X\rightarrow Y, which means if X holds, then Y also holds, where X and Y can be single or multiple variables with a truth value. In order to apply ARM methods to numerical data, many approaches have been proposed, including discretization, optimization and statistical approaches, under the name Numerical ARM or Quantitative ARM [3]. As an example, for time series data produced by IoT devices, a simple association rule based on a statistical approach can be in the form \text{mean}(m_{t}^{X})\rightarrow\text{mean}(n_{t}^{Y}), which is interpreted as "in a time frame t, if mean measurement from sensor X is m, then the mean value of the measurements of sensor Y must be n". Discretization methods refer to discretizing numerical data before running an ARM algorithm. Optimization methods refer to evolutionary algorithms where rule quality criteria are generally used as fitness functions to learn rules in a desired format [3].

We hypothesize that for numerical data produced in industrial IoT networks, incorporating the semantics of system components in rule learning can be beneficial, including discovering previously unknown relations, e.g. a higher number of rules, and helping to generalize association rules of the above form. This hypothesis is tested in a specific type of IoT scenario, a Digital Twin (DT). DTs have had many different proposed definitions over the past two decades [4]. The main goal is to create a precise representation ('twin') of a physical system, often referred to as the Physical Twin (PT), in a digital environment and to maintain bi-directional communication between them. Recently, semantic technologies such as ontologies and Knowledge Graphs (KGs) have started to be used in DTs for system/data modeling, establishing semantic interoperability, extracting semantic relations and/or facilitating reasoning processes [5].

To the best of our knowledge, at the time of writing, there is no approach for learning rules containing semantic information as well as time series data in a DT. This study aims to fill this gap by proposing a first semantic rule learning approach utilizing KGs, based on the well-known FP-Growth [6] algorithm. Concretely, the contributions of this paper are as follows:

- • Describing a full pipeline of operations that consists of: i) KG construction in DTs, ii) semantic association rule learning based on the KG and time series data, and iii) making inferences based on the learned rules (Section 2).

- • A first approach (Naive SemRL) that extends the FP-Growth algorithm to learn rules containing semantic information from KGs and time-series data (Section 3).

- • A semantic rule quality measure to evaluate rules generated by semantic rule learning algorithms (Section 4).

The proposed approach is evaluated in an industrial use case, water networks, i.e. water distribution systems that bring water to consumers, such as apartments and industrial sites. This is ongoing research with many open issues and research questions, which are emphasized in Section 5.
